transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah… I came in because I feel like I’m losing these big chunks of time to checking things over and over, but not exactly checking like… I don’t know, a stove or something. It’s more like I’ll re-read emails and texts again and again, or I’ll reopen the same work folders repeatedly, and I’ll sit there mentally replaying conversations before I can leave the house or really start working.

It’s like I’m trying to prove to myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake — that I didn’t write something wrong, miss something important, say something that could be taken badly, or leave some file in the wrong place. And I know from the outside it probably looks unnecessary, because I may have already looked at it, but I don’t feel settled. I’ll think, “Okay, just one more time,” and then that turns into another pass, and another. It eats up time, and by the time I actually start the thing I meant to do, I’m already tired or late or frustrated with myself.
Can you tell me if you have thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want or that bother you — maybe thoughts that feel out of line with who you are or what you believe in?

Yes. That’s actually a big part of what’s been happening. It’s not like I sit down and decide to worry about these things — they just barge in, usually at the worst times.

Like, I’ll be trying to work through a system design problem, or I’ll be preparing a lesson or organizing something in my head, and suddenly there’s this thought like, “What if you sent the wrong message to your ex-wife?” Or, “What if you mishandled those family photos somehow?” Or, “What if you let someone in the community down and you’re just not remembering it right?” And then it sort of grabs onto me.

The frustrating part is that I’ll know, at least logically, that I’ve already been over it. I’ll think, “No, you checked that,” or “You thought through that already,” but it doesn’t feel finished. It feels like if I don’t stop and go back over it again, I might be ignoring something important or irresponsible. And it’s very much not how I want to be spending my mind, if that makes sense. It feels intrusive — like it doesn’t belong there, but I can’t just let it pass.
When these intrusive thoughts come up, do you feel driven to do something — either physically or mentally — to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Yes, I do. It’s not always a big obvious thing like getting up and touching something, although sometimes it’s physical in the sense that I’ll actually reopen things. But a lot of it is this… this need to verify.

So if the thought is, “What if I wrote something wrong?” then I’ll go back and re-read the email or the text. Not just once, usually. I’ll read it, feel okay for maybe a second, and then there’s this little doubt — like maybe I skimmed it too fast, or maybe I missed the one sentence that matters — and then I read it again. And sometimes I’m not even reading normally anymore, I’m sort of scanning for danger, if that makes sense.

With work files, I’ll reopen the same folders or documents to make sure I put something where it belongs or didn’t overlook something important. I know I was just in the folder. I know I probably saw what I needed to see. But the feeling doesn’t leave unless I go back in again, and even then it may only quiet down briefly.

And mentally, I do the same thing with conversations. Before I leave the house or before I can really settle into work, I’ll replay what I said to someone, almost like I’m reviewing a recording in my head, trying to prove I didn’t say something careless or make some serious mistake. It’s exhausting because it feels like I’m trying to get certainty, and I can’t quite get it. I tell myself, “Just check once more so you can move on,” but then the “once more” doesn’t stay once.

When you go back and re-read emails, reopen files, or mentally replay conversations, is it specifically to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce the anxiety that comes with these intrusive thoughts?

Yes… yes, that’s pretty much exactly what it is. It’s not that I’m enjoying the checking or that I think it’s useful in some normal, practical way. It’s more like I get this spike of anxiety — this feeling that I may have missed something serious — and then going back over the email or the folder or the conversation feels like the only way to bring that feeling down.

I’ll tell myself, “Just confirm it and then you can move on.” Like if I re-read the message one more time, I’ll finally be sure I didn’t say something wrong. Or if I reopen the folder again, I’ll be able to prove to myself I didn’t put something in the wrong place or overlook something important. And with conversations, I’ll mentally replay them before leaving the house or before starting work because I’m trying to reassure myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake.

But the relief is usually temporary. I might feel okay for a moment, and then the doubt comes back, and I think, “Wait, did I really check carefully enough?” So yes, it’s mainly to reduce that anxiety and to prevent the possibility — or the feeling of the possibility — that something bad could happen because I missed something.

When you re-read emails, reopen files, or mentally replay conversations, do you feel that you have to do it a certain number of times or in a specific way — like until it feels 'just right' or you get a sense of completion — even if you can't explain exactly why?

Yes… not always a clean number, like “exactly five times,” but it does have to feel complete. That’s the part that’s hard to explain without sounding ridiculous.

I might re-read an email and technically I can see it’s fine, but if I didn’t read it in the right way — like slowly enough, or with enough attention, or I feel like I rushed past a sentence — then it doesn’t count in my mind. So I start again. And with folders, I’ll reopen them because I want that feeling of, “Okay, yes, I’ve proved it’s where it should be,” but if the feeling doesn’t land, I keep going.

It’s the same with replaying conversations. Before I leave the house or start work, I’ll run through what I said, trying to prove to myself I didn’t make some serious mistake. And if the replay feels fuzzy or I can’t remember the exact wording, then I get pulled back into it again.

That’s actually a lot of why I came in — I keep losing chunks of time to re-reading emails and texts, reopening folders, and going back over conversations in my head. It’s like I’m chasing this sense of certainty or completion, and sometimes I get it for a second, but it doesn’t hold very well.

Can you tell me if these behaviors or mental acts, like re-reading emails or replaying conversations, feel necessary to prevent something bad from happening or to stop yourself from feeling so anxious?

Yes. That’s really the heart of it, I think. It feels necessary, even when I know, logically, that rereading the same email again probably isn’t going to reveal some completely new thing.

I came in because I keep losing chunks of time to it — rereading emails and texts, reopening folders, going back into documents I already checked — and then also doing it in my head with conversations. Like before I leave the house or before I really start work, I’ll mentally replay what I said to someone, trying to prove to myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake.

It’s not just “being careful.” It feels more urgent than that. It’s like if I don’t check, or if I don’t replay it clearly enough, then I’m left with this awful feeling that maybe I missed something important and something bad could come from it. And the checking is supposed to make that feeling stop. Sometimes it does for a minute, but then the doubt comes back and I get pulled into doing it again.

Do you feel that your checking behaviors or mental acts have to be done in a certain way or according to specific rules — like needing to read the email perfectly or replay the conversation exactly in your mind — even if you can’t quite explain why it has to be that way?

Yes… yes, it does feel that way. It’s not always a formal rule, like I’ve written it down or anything, but there’s definitely a “right” way my mind wants it done.

With emails or texts, I can’t just glance back and be satisfied. I’ll feel like I need to read it properly — every line, sometimes almost every word — and if my attention drifts for even a second, then it’s like it didn’t count. I’ll think, “No, you didn’t really check that.” So I start over, even though I’ve already seen it.

And with files or folders, I’ll reopen something I already checked because I don’t feel convinced. I’ll look again to make sure it’s in the right place or that I didn’t miss something, but if I don’t get that certain feeling — that feeling of, “Okay, now I know” — then I keep going back.

The mental replaying is probably the hardest to explain. Before I leave the house or start work, I’ll run conversations back in my head, trying to prove to myself I didn’t make some serious mistake. And if I can’t remember it clearly enough, or if the sequence feels off, or I think I may have skipped over something important, then I’ll replay it again. It’s like I’m trying to get it exactly clear enough that my brain will let me move on.

I know it sounds excessive, but it really feels like unless I do it in that particular way, the checking hasn’t actually been completed.
